summary: North Korea is essentially closed to tourism: borders shut in 2020 and have reopened only for limited, state-organized group tours aimed chiefly at the Russian market. Every visitor needs a visa arranged through a state-approved tour operator, independent travel is impossible, and US and South Korean passport holders cannot visit at all.

travelInsurance.text: Not formally published as an entry requirement, but tour operators generally insist on comprehensive travel insurance — medical facilities are very limited and evacuation is slow and difficult.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the DPRK

onwardTicket.text: All travel is on a fixed itinerary booked through the tour operator, normally via Beijing or Vladivostok — independent arrival or departure is not possible.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the DPRK

proofOfFunds.text: No proof-of-funds check applies — tours are prepaid packages and visitors have no access to local banking.

declarations.name: Arrival customs declaration
declarations.text: All visitors complete a written customs declaration on arrival listing electronic devices, published material and foreign currency; devices and reading material may be inspected.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the DPRK

currencyLimits.text: Foreign currency must be declared on arrival. North Korean won (KPW) may not be imported or exported — visitors pay for everything in euros, US dollars or Chinese yuan in cash.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the DPRK

notes: Religious literature, South Korean media and any material deemed critical of the state are strictly prohibited — bringing them in can lead to detention.
Satellite phones and GPS devices must be declared and may be held at the border until departure; mobile phones are usually admitted but local networks are inaccessible to visitors.
Photography is tightly controlled — photograph only where your guides permit, and expect cameras to be checked on exit.

payments.text: Foreign cards do not work anywhere and there are no accessible ATMs. Bring everything you will spend as cash in euros, US dollars or Chinese yuan, in small denominations. Visitors generally cannot use the local won.

safety.text: Foreign governments advise against all travel to North Korea. The risk of arbitrary arrest and long-term detention is real, consular assistance is minimal or non-existent, and visitors must follow state rules and their guides' instructions at all times.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — North Korea Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: Spring and fall offer mild, clear weather for Pyongyang and countryside excursions; tours also cluster around major state holidays such as the mid-April celebrations.

tips.text: Most Western governments advise against all travel to North Korea, citing the serious risk of arbitrary arrest and long-term detention. US passports cannot be used for travel there at all under US law.
Never leave your group, photograph without permission, fold or deface images of the leaders, or bring religious or South Korean material — behavior that seems trivial elsewhere can lead to detention.

Tourism has been essentially closed since January 2020. A brief reopening for Western tourists via Rason in early 2025 was suspended within weeks; only limited Russian-market group tours run with any regularity — status changes with little notice.
Expect to be offline for the whole trip — visitors have no internet access and no usable mobile network. Tell family and colleagues in advance.
Bring small-denomination euros, US dollars or Chinese yuan in good condition — change is scarce and worn notes may be refused.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for North Korea?
faq.answer: Yes — every visitor needs a visa, and it can only be arranged through a state-approved tour operator as part of an organized, guided tour. In practice tourism has been essentially closed since 2020, with only limited group tours (mainly for the Russian market) resuming. US and South Korean passport holders cannot visit at all.

faq.question: Can US citizens visit North Korea?
faq.answer: No. The restriction comes from the US side: since 2017 US law has declared US passports invalid for travel to, in or through North Korea unless specially validated by the State Department — validations are granted only in very narrow cases such as journalism or humanitarian work.

faq.question: Is North Korea open to tourists in 2026?
faq.answer: Barely. Borders closed in January 2020 and general tourism has not resumed. Limited Russian group tours restarted in 2024, and a brief reopening for other nationalities via the Rason zone in early 2025 was suspended after a few weeks. Anyone considering a trip should check the current position with a specialist tour operator.

faq.question: Can I travel independently in North Korea?
faq.answer: No. All visits are guided group or private tours with state-approved guides accompanying you at all times; you cannot choose your own itinerary, wander unaccompanied or use local transport independently.

faq.question: What money do tourists use in North Korea?
faq.answer: Cash only — euros, US dollars and Chinese yuan are all accepted at hotels and tourist venues. Foreign cards and ATMs do not work, and visitors are generally not permitted to hold or export the local won (KPW).
